practice.title: 5 habits to progress faster on your instrument
practice.excerpt: A little every day beats a marathon on Sunday. Here's how to structure effective practice, even with just 15 minutes.
body: Consistency beats intensity: 15 minutes every day moves you further than a two-hour session once a week. The brain consolidates a technical gesture during the sleep that follows practice — spreading sessions out means more nights of consolidation.

Split each session into three short parts: a technical warm-up, focused work on one specific point (a tricky passage, a rhythm), then a moment of pure enjoyment replaying what you already master. That last part is what makes you want to come back tomorrow.
Finally, record yourself once a week. You improve faster when you actually hear yourself play, not just how you feel while playing.

sound.title: Sound engineering: where do you even start?
sound.excerpt: Recording, mixing, mastering: an overview to understand the craft and choose your specialization.
body: Sound engineering actually covers several distinct crafts: recording (capturing an instrument or voice under the best conditions), mixing (balancing and shaping tracks together), and mastering (finalizing a track's overall sound). Many beginners try to learn everything at once — it's better to pick one entry point.

If you like hands-on, in-the-room work, start with recording: it trains you to listen before you manipulate. If you prefer composing and arranging, mixing will feel more natural. Mastering almost always comes last, once your ear is already trained.
Gear isn't everything: critical listening, developed on headphones or speakers you know inside out, matters more than a high-end mixing console when you're starting out.

heritage.title: Why passing on traditional African instruments matters
heritage.excerpt: Kora, djembe, balafon: Africa's musical heritage is being passed on online too. Meet the teachers behind it.
body: For centuries, these instruments were passed on almost exclusively in person, often within the same family or community. That oral transmission is precious, but it also limits how many people can learn, especially far from where these skills are still practiced daily.

Online lessons don't replace that direct transmission, but they open an extra door: a student in Yaoundé can learn balafon from a teacher in Mali; someone in the diaspora can reconnect with an instrument their family hasn't played in two generations.
That's the whole point of AfriSon Academy's traditional instruments section: giving teachers the means to pass on their craft beyond their own geographic circle, without distorting what they teach.
